sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Two strings are anagrams when they contain the same symbols with the same frequencies under the agreed normalization rules. Order does not matter, but duplicate counts do.

Count every rune in the first string, subtract counts while scanning the second, and reject a missing or exhausted count. A remaining non-zero count means the inputs differ.

For example, `listen` and `silent` each contain one of the same six letters. By contrast, `aab` and `abb` use the same set of letters but different frequencies, so they are not anagrams.

The caller must decide whether spaces, punctuation, letter case, and canonically equivalent Unicode forms are significant. Lowercasing alone is not a complete language-independent normalization rule.

A rune-frequency map is a strong default when input may contain Unicode and the check should run in linear time. A fixed array is faster only when the alphabet is small and guaranteed.
